notes.text: By way of the Red-sea — Which leadeth to the Red-sea, as they must needs do to compass the land of Edom. Because of the way - By reason of this journey, which was long and troublesome, and unexpected, because the successful entrance and victorious progress which some of them had made in the borders of Canaan, made them think they might have speedily gone in and taken possession of it, and so have saved the tedious travels and farther difficulties, into which Moses had again brought them.

Against God — Against Christ, their chief conductor, whom they tempted, 1 Cor. x, 19. Thus contemptuously did they speak of Manna, whereas it appears it yielded excellent nourishment, because in the strength of it they were able to go so many and such tedious journeys.

Fiery serpents — There were many such in this wilderness, which having been hitherto restrained by God, are now let loose and sent among them. They are called fiery from their effects, because their poison caused an intolerable heat and burning and thirst, which was aggravated with this circumstance of the place, that here was no water, ver. 5.

A fiery serpent — That is, the figure of a serpent in brass, which is of a fiery colour. This would require some time: God would not speedily take off the judgment, because he saw they were not throughly humbled. Upon a pole - That the people might see it from all parts of the camp, and therefore the pole must be high, and the serpent large. When he looketh -This method of cure was prescribed, that it might appear to be God's own work, and not the effect of nature or art: and that it might be an eminent type of our salvation by Christ. The serpent signified Christ, who was in the likeness of sinful flesh, though without sin, as this brazen serpent had the outward shape, but not the inward poison, of the other serpents: the pole resembled the cross upon which Christ was lifted up for our salvation: and looking up to it designed our believing in Christ.
He lived — He was delivered from death, and cured of his disease.

glossa.text: *They set forward,* etc. ((HIERON., epist. ad Fabiolam. )) The thirty-fifth station, etc., *as far as* but with the mouth confession unto salvation ((Rom. X)).

*Make a serpent ((ISID. in Num., tom. V.))* Those bitten by the serpents were healed when the brazen serpent was lifted up and looked upon, etc., *as far as* he lives through his Divinity as though of brass.

notes.text: Gathered — Into their own land.

glossa.text:
*Give praise to the Lord.* ((ID.)) This psalm teaches what we are through ourselves, etc., *as far as* he first admonishes the redeemed to give praise. *Give praise.*

((CASS., AUG.)) Of which there are seven divisions, etc., *as far as* in the seventh he treats of heretics, there, *And they were made few.*
*And from the sea.* ((CASS.)) For the south he puts the sea, understanding thereby the ocean of that quarter; and this can be taken for any quarter of the world whatever.

notes.text: And he hath quickened you — In the nineteenth and twentieth verses of the preceding chapter, St. Paul spoke of God's working in them by the same almighty power whereby he raised Christ from the dead. On the mention of this he, in the fulness of his heart, runs into a flow of thought concerning the glory of Christ's exaltation in the three following verses. He here resumes the thread of his discourse. Who were dead - Not only diseased, but dead; absolutely void of all spiritual life; and as incapable of quickening yourselves, as persons literally dead. In trespasses and sins-Sins seem to be spoken chiefly of the gentiles, who knew not God; trespasses, of the Jews, who had his law, and yet regarded it not, ver. 5. The latter herein obeyed the flesh; the former, the prince of the power of the air.

According to the course of this world — The word translated course properly means a long series of times, wherein one corrupt age follows another. According to the prince of the power of the air - The effect of which power all may perceive, though all do not understand the cause of it: a power unspeakably penetrating and widely diffused; but yet, as to its baneful influences, beneath the orb of believers. The evil spirits are united under one head, the seat of whose dominion is in the air. Here he sometimes raises storms, sometimes makes visionary representations, and is continually roving to and fro. The spirit that now worketh - With mighty power; and so he did, and doth in all ages. In the sons of disobedience - In all who do not believe and obey the gospel.

Among whom we — Jews. Also, formerly had our conversation: doing the will of the flesh - In gross, brutal sins. And of the mind - By spiritual, diabolical wickedness. In the former clause, flesh denotes the whole evil nature; in the latter, the body opposed to the soul. And were by nature - That is, in our natural state. Children of wrath - Having the wrath of God abiding on us, even as the gentiles. This expression, by nature, occurs also, Gal. iv, 8; Rom. ii, 14; and thrice in the eleventh chapter. But in none of these places does it signify, by custom, or practice, or customary practice, as a late writer affirms. Nor can it mean so here For this would make the apostle guilty of gross tautology, their customary sinning having been expressed already, in the former part of the verse. But all these passages agree in expressing what belongs to the nature of the persons spoken of.
Mercy removes misery: love confers salvation.

He hath quickened us together with Christ — In conformity to him, and by virtue of our union with him. By grace ye are saved - Grace is both the beginning and end. The apostle speaks indifferently either in the first or second person; the Jews and gentiles being in the same circumstance, both by nature and by grace. This text lays the axe to the very root of spiritual pride, and all glorying in ourselves. Therefore St. Paul, foreseeing the backwardness of mankind to receive it, yet knowing the absolute necessity of its being received, again asserts the very same truth, ver. 8, in the very same words.

And hath raised us up together — Both Jews and gentiles already in spirit; and ere long our bodies too will be raised. And made us all sit together in heavenly places - This is spoken by way of anticipation. Believers are not yet possessed of their seats in heaven; but each of them has a place prepared for him.
The ages to come — That is, all succeeding ages.

By grace ye are saved through faith — Grace, without any respect to human worthiness, confers the glorious gift. Faith, with an empty hand, and without any pretense to personal desert, receives the heavenly blessing. And this is not of yourselves - This refers to the whole preceding clause, That ye are saved through faith, is the gift of God.
Not by works — Neither this faith nor this salvation is owing to any works you ever did, will, or can do.

For we are his workmanship — Which proves both that salvation is by faith, and that faith is the gift of God. Created unto good works - That afterwards we might give ourselves to them. Which God had before preprepared - The occasions of them: so we must still ascribe the whole to God. That we might walk in them - Though not be justified by them.

glossa.text: *And you, when you were,* etc. He calls to mind former things, that in good things they may be humbled, and that it may be certain that if these things were given to enemies, they shall the more be given to friends, which the Apostle desires; as if he should say: He is the head of the whole Church and yours, because he hath quickened you together: when, that is, although you were dead. Or we who have believed have the hope of the inheritance, and you also, that is, you have believed. But God quickened you together, or raised up Jesus, etc.

*The prince.* Namely Beelzebub, who is the prince of the malignant spirits, or, intransitively, the prince of spirits. He calls the prince of error the spirit of the air, in which he bears rule. *Of the air.* The murky lower air is that of the demons. *Of the spirit.* That is, of spirits: for the genitive singular is put for the plural. *Who worketh in the children of unbelief.* What? if not his own evil works: and among the first chiefly, because that very unbelief and infidelity by which they are enemies of the faith, through whom he knows that they can be cleansed?

*And we were by nature,* etc. As if: since these foresaid things were in us, let not the Gentile despair but that he may become equal to the Jews. *Children of wrath.* Mortals are born with the wrath of God, because, Adam sinning, vice grew in place of nature. For the human race was held under a just damnation, and all were by nature children of wrath.
*He hath quickened us together.* Or us Jews, and you Gentiles likewise, and this is: by whose grace you Gentiles are saved. And he raised up both together.

*He hath made to sit together,* etc. Not vainly, but faithfully, he already reckons as done that which he does not doubt shall be. For certainly Christ already sits in the heavenly places, but we not yet; yet we hold it by a sure hope.

*In the ages to come, abounding,* etc. For in the age to come the gift of God shall appear, in the remuneration of believers; which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard. And these are the abounding riches, that so much be given as the mind cannot search out.

*And this not of yourselves,* etc. Lest perchance thou say: I have deserved it, therefore I received it. Do not think that thou hast received by deserving. Grace went before thy merit: not grace from merit, but merit from grace. For if grace were from merit, thou hast bought it, thou hast not received it freely. Grace goes before all merits, so that my merits may follow the gifts of God.

*That no man may glory.* He does not say this for the reason that good works done with a pious thought are made void, since God renders to every man according to his works, and there is glory of God to him that works good, but because works are from grace, not grace from works. It is good, therefore, for a man that he presume not upon the powers of his own will; because he who thought that without his help he could keep what he had given, having set out into a far country, and living prodigally, consumed all: and, worn down by misery, and returned into himself, said: *I will arise, and I will go to my father ((Luc. XV))*. Which good thought he would not have had, unless the most merciful Father had inspired that very thing into him in secret.

*For we are his,* etc. No one ought to glory, because we, created in faith and in works, are his making, that is, his work, or we are created through his making, that is, his operation: and so neither must one glory of works through faith, since faith and all things are from grace.

notes.text: And as Moses — And even this single witness will soon be taken from you; yea, and in a most ignominious manner. Num. xxi, 8, 9.

That whosoever — He must be lifted up, that hereby he may purchase salvation for all believers: all those who look to him by faith recover spiritual health, even as all that looked at that serpent recovered bodily health.

Yea, and this was the very design of God's love in sending him into the world. Whosoever believeth on him — With that faith which worketh by love, and hold fast the beginning of his confidence steadfast to the end. God so loved the world - That is, all men under heaven; even those that despise his love, and will for that cause finally perish. Otherwise not to believe would be no sin to them. For what should they believe? Ought they to believe that Christ was given for them? Then he was given for them. He gave his only Son - Truly and seriously. And the Son of God gave himself, Gal. iv, 4, truly and seriously.
God sent not his Son into the world to condemn the world — Although many accuse him of it.

He that believeth on him is not condemned — Is acquitted, is justified before God. The name of the only-begotten Son of God - The name of a person is often put for the person himself. But perhaps it is farther intimated in that expression, that the person spoken of is great and magnificent. And therefore it is generally used to express either God the Father or the Son.
This is the condemnation — That is, the cause of it. So God is clear.
He that practiceth the truth (that is, true religion) cometh to the light — So even Nicodemus, afterward did. Are wrought in God - That is, in the light, power, and love of God.

glossa.text: *And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert.* He puts forward his own death, which is the origin and the cause of having the things aforesaid, and in faith of it he instructs him. And because he was carnal, and versed in the law, therefore he brings forward a certain part of the law, which he shows to be a figure and significative of his own death, so that in this way it may be plain of the other parts of the law also that they are in figure. And because death is understood by the serpent, and Christ dead is called a serpent, whom he who beholds with faith is set free; as by the beholding of that other one in the figure they are set free from the fiery serpents, which signify the incitements of the vices. *So must the Son of man be lifted up,* etc. He invites the master of the law to the signification of the law. And because he had spoken of the Son of man, lest Nicodemus should think this only, he subjoins that the same is also the Son of God. *For God so loved.* He opens the cause of human salvation, namely, the love of God the Father, from whom all restoration is through his Son in the Holy Spirit.

*The world.* Cosmos in Greek, which in Latin is rendered *mundus*, is called adornment. By the world, therefore, human nature is signified, not because according to the body it consists of the four elements, but because according to the soul it has been adorned by God and made to the image of God; wherefore God loves it to this end, that he may make it eternal.

*That he would give his only-begotten Son, that everyone who believes,* etc. Behold, he says the same of the Son of God which he said above of the Son of man, so that by him through whom we were founded in the deity, through the same we may be restored in the man.

*And this is the judgment.* Why is he who does not believe judged? Because the light came which rouses men and admonishes them to know their own evils, in which all men are; but some hate the light that admonishes, and flee, lest their evils which they love should be reproved. Others, admonished by the light, accuse their own evils, which is to do the truth, and so they are enlightened. *For theirs were.* He who is in darkness and loves the light is not evil; but he is called evil, and his works evil, who, after the light has come, hates the light and loves evil things And this is what he says: *For their works were evil.* Works, that is, impiety, and unbelief, and hatred of the eternal light, and the unwillingness to look upon it, but the will to remain in the darkness of sins.

*But he that doeth.* Having shown by what justice he is condemned who does not believe, he shows by what justice he is saved who believes. *But he that doeth.* That is, he to whom his own evils are displeasing, and who accuses them, does not pardon himself, does not spare himself, but comes to the light. And he begins to act with God who accuses his own evils, because the beginning of good is the accusation of evil. Therefore his works, these namely, that he accuses himself as God accuses, he manifests, because they are done in God; for unless the light of God shone upon him, he would not be displeasing to himself.

echoes.text: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
echoes.note: 'Dead in transgressions and sins' draws on the Edenic verdict that disobedience brings death ('in the day you eat of it you shall surely die'). The metaphor of spiritual death as the consequence of sin coheres with Genesis' linkage of transgression and death, an availability Paul could presume.

echoes.text: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden?’” The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.’” The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t surely […]
echoes.note: The serpent's deception inaugurating human disobedience underlies 'children of disobedience' and the death-through-sin pattern. The figural Adam/Eden background coheres with Paul's broader use of the Fall narrative elsewhere.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: 'The prince of the power of the air' presupposes a heavenly accusing spirit-figure like the satan who roams and acts in the world. Job's Adversary supplies an available OT prototype for a malign cosmic ruler operating under God, though no verbal link exists.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: 'Doing the desires of the flesh and of the mind' echoes the flood-era verdict that every inclination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil. The OT yetzer-language of corrupt human imagination coheres with Paul's 'desires of the mind.'

echoes.text: Behold, I was born in iniquity. In sin my mother conceived me.
echoes.note: 'By nature children of wrath' resonates with the Psalmist's confession of being conceived in sin, supplying OT warrant for an innate sinful condition. The coherence is thematic (inborn guilt) rather than verbal.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: 'God, being rich in mercy, for his great love' draws directly on the Sinai self-revelation of YHWH as 'merciful and gracious... abounding in steadfast love.' The pairing of abundant mercy with great love reproduces the chesed-rab formula, a high-volume, recurrent OT confession Paul evokes to ground salvation in God's covenant character.

echoes.text: Yahweh is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness.
echoes.note: 'Rich in mercy... great love' echoes the Psalm's restatement of the Exodus 34 formula, 'The LORD is merciful and gracious... abounding in steadfast love.' Recurrence of this confession in the Psalter strengthens the allusion as the lens through which Paul reads God's saving initiative.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: Being 'raised up with him and made to sit with him in the heavenly places' applies the enthronement oracle 'Sit at my right hand' to believers' co-exaltation with Christ. Psalm 110:1 is the most-cited OT verse in the NT, and its session-language coheres precisely with Paul's seating motif.

echoes.text: My God, turn your ear, and hear; open your eyes, and see our desolations, and the city which is called by your name: for we do not present our petitions before you for our righteousness, but for your great mercies’ sake.
echoes.note: Salvation grounded 'not on our own righteousness but on God's great mercy' parallels Daniel's plea appealing to God's great mercy rather than human merit. The coherence with 2:4-9's grace-not-works logic is notable though verbally faint.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Not of works, that no one would boast' invokes the prophetic prohibition against self-boasting: 'Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom... but let him who boasts boast in this, that he knows me.' Paul cites this exact text elsewhere (1 Cor 1:31), making it the controlling OT warrant for excluding human boasting before God.

echoes.text: Don’t say in your heart, after Yahweh your God has thrust them out from before you, saying, “For my righteousness Yahweh has brought me in to possess this land”; because Yahweh drives them out before you because of the wickedness of these nations. Not for your righteousness, or for the uprightness of your heart, do you go in to possess their land; but for the wickedness of these nations Yahweh your God does drive them out from before you, and that he may […]
echoes.note: 'Not of yourselves... not of works' echoes Moses' insistence that Israel possesses the land 'not because of your righteousness' but by God's gift. The covenantal grace-not-merit logic coheres tightly with Paul's anti-works argument.

echoes.text: Those who trust in their wealth, and boast in the multitude of their riches— none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him.
echoes.note: The futility of boasting in wealth or self-ransom ('no man can redeem... or give to God a ransom for him') resonates with salvation as God's gift, not human achievement. The link to 2:9's no-boasting is thematic and faint.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
echoes.note: 'His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus' deploys creation-language (ktizo/bara) to frame redemption as a new creative act of God. The Genesis creation account is the figural backdrop for the 'created... for good works' new-creation motif.

echoes.text: Know that Yahweh, he is God. It is he who has made us, and we are his. We are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
echoes.note: 'We are his workmanship' echoes 'It is he who made us, and we are his' — the confession of God as maker of his people. The coherence with creaturely dependence on the Maker reinforces the new-creation reading.

echoes.text: But when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in the midst of him, they will sanctify my name. Yes, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and will stand in awe of the God of Israel.
echoes.note: 'The work of my hands... they will sanctify my name' resonates with believers as God's 'workmanship... for good works.' Isaiah's restoration-as-recreation theme coheres with Paul's eschatological new making.

echoes.text: the people which I formed for myself, that they might declare my praise.
echoes.note: 'The people I formed for myself, that they might declare my praise' parallels a people created for a purpose (good works). The purposive creation-language coheres with 2:10 though no verbal quotation occurs.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.
echoes.note: The explicit typological centerpiece: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up.' Direct verbal and figural correspondence — the lifted bronze serpent that the snake-bitten looked to and lived prefigures the crucified Son giving eternal life to those who believe. Maximal volume and coherence.

echoes.text: For even when terrible raging of wild beasts came upon your people, And they were perishing by the bites of crooked serpents, Your wrath continued not to the uttermost; But for admonition were they troubled for a short space, Having a token of salvation, To put them in remembrance of the commandment of your law: For he that turned toward it was not saved because of that which was seen, But because of you, the Saviour of all.
echoes.note: The Wisdom midrash on Numbers 21 clarifies that 'the one who turned toward it was saved, not by what was seen, but by you, the Savior of all' — exactly John's point that the serpent saves by directing faith beyond itself to God. Strong Second-Temple interpretive parallel, high coherence with 3:15's believing-and-living.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: The Servant who is 'lifted up (hypsothesetai) and exalted' supplies the double sense of John's hypsoo (crucified/exalted) Son of Man. LXX verbal contact with the lifting-up vocabulary that John deploys here and in 8:28; 12:32-34.

echoes.text: He removed the high places, and broke the pillars, and cut down the Asherah: and he broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made; for in those days the children of Israel burned incense to it; and he called it Nehushtan.
echoes.note: Hezekiah's destruction of the bronze serpent (Nehushtan) is part of the object's canonical afterlife and may inform the careful 'not the bronze itself but faith' nuance; faint, supplementary to Num 21.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: 'God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son' echoes the Aqedah where God says of Isaac 'your son, your only son, whom you love' and credits Abraham who 'did not withhold' him. The LXX agapetos / monogenes-equivalent and the giving of the beloved only son give strong figural volume and coherence.

echoes.text: “Arise, shine; for your light has come, and Yahweh’s glory is risen on you. For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but Yahweh will arise on you, and his glory shall be seen on you. Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising.
echoes.note: 'The light has come into the world' and nations coming to the light coheres with Isaiah's 'Arise, shine, for your light has come.' Recurrent Johannine light-coming-into-the-world motif (cf. 1:9; 8:12); moderate verbal contact.

echoes.text: “These are of those who rebel against the light. They don’t know its ways, nor stay in its paths. The murderer rises with the light. He kills the poor and needy. In the night he is like a thief. The eye also of the adulterer waits for the twilight, saying, ‘No eye shall see me.’ He disguises his face. In the dark they dig through houses. They shut themselves up in the daytime. They don’t know the light. For the morning is to all of them like thick […]
echoes.note: The evildoers who 'rebel against the light,' who do their deeds in darkness and for whom 'morning is like deep darkness,' closely parallel 3:19-20: those who do evil hate the light lest their works be exposed. Strong thematic coherence of light/darkness moral exposure.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: 'The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light' supplies the light-into-darkness frame of 3:19; faint, part of the broader Isaianic light cluster.

echoes.text: For whoever finds me, finds life, and will obtain favor from Yahweh. But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul. All those who hate me love death.”
echoes.note: 'Whoever finds me finds life... all who hate me love death' parallels the believe-and-live / hate-the-light-love-darkness antithesis of 3:16-20 in a wisdom register; faint.

echoes.text: But for admonition were they troubled for a short space, Having a token of salvation, To put them in remembrance of the commandment of your law: For he that turned toward it was not saved because of that which was seen, But because of you, the Saviour of all.
echoes.note: The salvific 'looking' that brings life carries over from 3:14-15 into the believing-for-eternal-life of 3:15-16; low independent volume here, recurrence within the pericope cluster.

echoes.text: Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
echoes.note: 'Their works were evil' (3:19) faintly recalls the flood-judgment verdict that human deeds were continually evil; low volume, judgment register.
